title: Twelfth Night
author: William Shakespeare
setting: Illyria: Orsino's court, Olivia's house and garden, and a stretch of coast
lengthNote: Around 2,500 lines, with more songs than any other Shakespeare comedy
openingLine: If music be the food of love, play on;
summary: A girl washed up in a country she has never heard of puts on her drowned brother's kind of clothes and goes to work for a duke. Everything that follows comes from that one decision: a messenger who is loved by the wrong person, a household whose joke ends in a man locked in a dark room, and a recognition scene that has to give two people back a twin before anybody can marry.

sourceText.label: Globe/Moby text of Twelfth Night
sourceText.note: Line numbers follow the traditional Globe numbering, which counts the prose scenes continuously. Modern editions vary.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: Probably composed in 1601, shortly before the earliest recorded performance.

atAGlance.label: First recorded performance
atAGlance.note: At Middle Temple Hall, noted in the diary of the law student John Manningham.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: The First Folio, among the comedies, as Twelfe Night, Or what you will.

atAGlance.label: Chief source
atAGlance.note: The twin-and-disguise story comes chiefly from 'Of Apolonius and Silla', part of a wider European tradition.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: The shipwreck, and Viola becomes Cesario
structure.summary: Orsino is in love with the idea of being in love; Olivia has sworn off company for seven years to mourn a brother. Viola, believing her own brother drowned, takes service with the duke as a boy called Cesario and is sent within three days to court the woman her master wants — a job she does well enough to be loved for it herself.

scenes.title: Music
scenes.summary: Orsino calls for a strain, tires of it in eight lines, and hears that Olivia will see nobody.

scenes.title: The coast
scenes.summary: Viola asks what country this is, is told her brother may have survived, and decides to serve disguised.

scenes.title: Late drinking
scenes.summary: Sir Toby introduces Sir Andrew as a suitor and as a source of income.

scenes.title: Three days in
scenes.summary: Cesario is already the duke's favourite and is sent to Olivia; Viola admits she wants the master.

scenes.title: The veil
scenes.summary: Feste talks his way back into favour; Olivia unveils for the messenger and falls in love with him.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: A ring, a night of songs, and a forged letter
structure.summary: Olivia sends a ring after Cesario on a pretext, and Viola understands her own position exactly: she loves Orsino, Orsino loves Olivia, Olivia loves a disguise. In the same act Malvolio interrupts a drinking party, and Maria answers him with a piece of handwriting designed to fit the fantasy he already has.

scenes.title: Sebastian lives
scenes.summary: Antonio, who has saved him from the sea, follows him into a city where he has enemies.

scenes.title: The ring
scenes.summary: Viola works out what Olivia has done and leaves the knot to time.

scenes.title: Cakes and ale
scenes.summary: A catch, a quarrel with the steward, and Maria's plan for the letter.

scenes.title: Patience on a monument
scenes.summary: Orsino discourses on men's constancy; Viola answers with a sister who never spoke.

scenes.title: The box-tree
scenes.summary: Malvolio reads the letter aloud while three men hide and provide the commentary.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: Yellow stockings, a duel and the wrong twin
structure.summary: Olivia abandons discretion and declares herself; Viola can say only that she is not what she is. Malvolio arrives smiling and cross-gartered in front of a woman in mourning and is taken for mad. Sir Toby arranges a duel between two people equally unwilling to fight it, and Antonio walks into the middle of it and is arrested.

scenes.title: Not what I am
scenes.summary: Feste on the abuse of words, and Olivia's open declaration to Cesario.

scenes.title: Sir Andrew's challenge
scenes.summary: Sir Toby dictates a letter so incoherent he decides to deliver the challenge by mouth.

scenes.title: The Elephant
scenes.summary: Antonio gives Sebastian his purse and arranges to meet him at an inn.

scenes.title: Madness
scenes.summary: The stockings, the dark room, the duel, and Antonio mistaking Viola for her brother.

structure.label: Act IV
structure.title: A beating, a betrothal and a dark room
structure.summary: Sebastian is attacked in the street by people who think they know him, is proposed to by a woman he has never met, and accepts. Malvolio, shut in the dark, is visited by Feste pretending to be a curate, who tells him the room is full of light. The comedy and the cruelty are running in the same scene.

scenes.title: Mistaken
scenes.summary: Sebastian fights Sir Andrew and Sir Toby; Olivia stops it and takes him home.

scenes.title: Sir Topas
scenes.summary: Feste in a false beard argues that there is no darkness but ignorance.

scenes.title: The chantry
scenes.summary: Sebastian, sure he is not mad, agrees to be betrothed on the spot.

structure.label: Act V
structure.title: The twins meet
structure.summary: Everything converges: Antonio's accusation, Olivia's claim to a husband, Orsino's threat to kill the boy he loves, and then Sebastian walks on. The knot unties itself in fifteen lines. Malvolio is released, reads his letter out, learns the truth and leaves promising revenge, and Feste is left alone to sing about rain.

scenes.title: Recognition
scenes.summary: The twins meet, three marriages are arranged, Malvolio exits vowing revenge, and the clown sings.

characters.name: Viola
characters.role: A shipwrecked gentlewoman, disguised as Cesario
characters.summary: She invents Cesario as a practical measure and then finds the disguise doing things she did not intend: it makes her the confidant of the man she loves and the object of the woman she is sent to persuade. She is the only character who sees the whole situation and the only one who can do nothing about it.
characters.clue: Washed ashore in a country she has never heard of, she dresses as her drowned brother's sort of young man and is sent to woo on behalf of the man she wants for herself.

relationships.label: courts for another, and is loved by

characters.name: Olivia
characters.summary: Her seven-year mourning is a position, and it lasts until somebody argues with her. Once she falls, she is the most decisive person in the play: she declares herself, sends after the messenger and marries a stranger within three days of meeting his face on somebody else.
characters.clue: She vows to weep for a brother for seven years, and is engaged to a man she has spoken to twice — and who is not the man she thinks.

relationships.label: loves, believing her a young man

characters.name: Orsino
characters.summary: He opens the play calling for music and stops it within eight lines, which is his whole character in one gesture. He has never spoken to Olivia; what he loves is the condition of loving, and the play transfers him to Viola with an ease that has troubled readers ever since.
characters.clue: He orders up music as an appetite to be killed by excess, courts a woman he never meets, and proposes to his own page in the last scene.

characters.name: Malvolio
characters.summary: Humourless, ambitious and correct about the drinking, which is what makes him unbearable. The trick works because the letter tells him what he already believes; the punishment goes far beyond the joke, and the play lets him leave without being forgiven or forgiving.
characters.clue: A steward who practises behaviour to his own shadow, appears before a woman in mourning in yellow stockings, and is shut in a dark room for smiling.

characters.name: Feste
characters.summary: He is paid by both households and belongs to neither, which lets him say things nobody else can. He sings the play's best songs, performs the curate who torments Malvolio, and is left alone at the end to sing about a world where it rains every day.
characters.clue: He is licensed to say anything, takes money from two rival houses, plays a priest in a false beard, and has the last word after everyone else has gone in to dinner.

characters.name: Sir Toby Belch
characters.summary: He lives in his niece's house at her expense and funds his drinking by keeping a rich fool on the premises. He is the engine of the misrule and the first to tire of it: when the duel goes wrong and he is bloodied, he turns on Sir Andrew and marries Maria offstage.
characters.clue: He keeps a foolish knight in the house for his money, argues that virtue does not abolish cakes and ale, and discards his friend the moment he gets hurt.

characters.name: Sir Andrew Aguecheek
characters.role: A foolish knight, Olivia's supposed suitor
characters.summary: He is being robbed in plain sight and is happy about it. Shakespeare gives him one line of real pathos — that he was adored once too — and then has him beaten by a stranger and cast off by the man who has been living on his money.
characters.clue: He is kept in the house as a suitor and a source of funds, is frightened into a duel he cannot fight, and says quietly that he was adored once.

characters.name: Maria
characters.summary: She writes the letter, and the letter is a piece of character analysis: she knows exactly what Malvolio wants to hear because she has watched him practise it. Her reward is marriage to Sir Toby, which happens offstage and is reported in a line.
characters.clue: She can imitate her mistress's hand closely enough to ruin a man, and her wages for it are a knight, announced in half a sentence.

characters.name: Sebastian
characters.summary: He arrives late, is given money by a man who loves him, and spends his scenes being greeted by strangers who know his name. Handed a countess, he does not question it; he checks that he is not mad, and marries her within the hour.
characters.clue: Everyone in the city seems to know him, one of them hits him and another proposes marriage, and he concludes that the air and the sun are at least real.

characters.name: Antonio
characters.summary: He risks arrest in a hostile city because he cannot stand to be parted from Sebastian, and says so in terms no other character in the play uses about anybody. He is arrested, believes himself betrayed, and at the end is neither punished nor paired: he simply stops speaking.
characters.clue: He follows a young man into a city where he is a wanted enemy, hands over his purse, and is left standing at the end with nothing settled.

themes.name: Desire and the imagined lover
themes.summary: Orsino has never met Olivia, Olivia falls for a messenger she sees for ten minutes, and Malvolio builds a marriage out of a letter with no name on it. The play's joke is that every one of them is in love with something they have made up, and that being right about the object is not what makes the feeling real.
themes.development: Orsino's abstract appetite in 1.1 becomes a proposal to a servant in 5.1, and the play does not stop to explain the transfer.

themes.name: Disguise and identity
themes.summary: Viola's costume is a practical solution that turns into a trap: it earns her the intimacy she wants and makes the declaration impossible. On a stage where the women were played by boys, a boy playing a girl playing a boy is a machine for saying true things under cover, more than a complication.
themes.development: She calls disguise a wickedness in 2.2, tells Olivia in 3.1 that she is not what she is, and never removes the clothes — the play ends with Orsino still calling her Cesario.

themes.name: Mourning and its uses
themes.summary: Two households are organised around a dead brother. Olivia's grief is public and performed for seven years; Viola's is private and she goes to work. The play is interested in the difference between grief you can display and grief you have to earn a living through.
themes.development: Both brothers turn out to be a matter of report — Sebastian is not dead, and Olivia's mourning ends the moment something more interesting arrives.

themes.name: Festivity and cruelty
themes.summary: Twelfth Night was the end of the Christmas misrule, and the play shows what happens when the licence runs on too long. The gulling of Malvolio is funny, then uncomfortable, then a man shut in the dark being told by a fake priest that the room is light.
themes.development: A catch sung at midnight in 2.3 leads by 4.2 to an imprisonment, and the household's response in 5.1 is that he brought it on himself.

themes.name: Service, rank and ambition
themes.summary: Almost everybody in Illyria works for somebody. Malvolio's offence is wanting to cross the line upward; Maria crosses it successfully by marrying Sir Toby, and nobody objects. The play punishes the ambition it finds humourless and rewards the one that makes people laugh.
themes.development: The letter's promise that some have greatness thrust upon them is quoted back at Malvolio by the fool in the last scene, after it has cost him everything.

themes.name: Time, patience and endings
themes.summary: Viola hands the knot to time because she can see no other way through, and time duly unties it by producing her brother. Nobody’s cleverness earns the comedy’s resolutions, which is part of why the last act feels magical and also slightly arbitrary.
themes.development: From ‘O time! thou must untangle this’ in 2.2 to the whirligig of time bringing in its revenges in 5.1, the play hands responsibility to the calendar.

techniques.name: Song
techniques.definition: Sung lyric used to carry mood, comment or structure, not plot.
techniques.inThisBook: There are more songs here than in any other Shakespeare comedy, and they go in one direction: from ‘O mistress mine’ through ‘Come away, death’ to a closing ballad about wind and rain that darkens the happy ending.

techniques.name: Speaking in disguise
techniques.definition: A character telling the literal truth in a form the listener cannot decode.
techniques.inThisBook: Viola's account of her father's daughter who never told her love is autobiography delivered to the man it is about, and he takes it as a story.

techniques.name: The gulling scene
techniques.definition: A trick staged in front of hidden observers who supply the running commentary.
techniques.inThisBook: The box-tree scene puts three men on stage interrupting a fourth as he reads, so that the audience laughs at the victim and at the watchers' inability to keep quiet.

techniques.name: Identical twins
techniques.definition: A plot device by which one actor's part is doubled by another body.
techniques.inThisBook: The device is old, but Shakespeare makes the twins brother and sister, so the resemblance depends on clothes, not nature — and that is the play’s point about gender, more than a mechanical convenience.

techniques.name: The licensed fool
techniques.definition: A professional entertainer permitted to say what others may not.
techniques.inThisBook: Feste’s wordplay on corruption and sentences is a job, not a temperament; Olivia defends him by saying there is no slander in an allowed fool, and he uses the permission to torment the one man who cannot laugh.

techniques.name: Prose and verse
techniques.definition: Movement between unmetered and metered speech as a signal of register or state.
techniques.inThisBook: The kitchen plot is almost all prose and the court scenes almost all verse; Malvolio's ruin is that he reads a prose letter as if it were a prophecy and then tries to talk like the people upstairs.

quotations.text: If music be the food of love, play on; Give me excess of it, that, surfeiting, The appetite may sicken, and so die.
quotations.speaker: Orsino
quotations.context: The first lines of the play, to his musicians.
quotations.analysis: He is not asking for music because he enjoys it; he wants to overeat until he is sick of the feeling. The metaphor treats love as an appetite that can be killed by indulgence, and eight lines later he stops the music because it is not as sweet as it was — an attention span the whole play measures him by.

quotations.text: What country, friends, is this?
quotations.speaker: Viola
quotations.context: Her first line, on the coast, having just survived the wreck.
quotations.analysis: Five words that establish everything: she has no idea where she is, no standing, and no information. The Captain's answer, 'This is Illyria, lady', is the last time anybody in the play addresses her as a woman until the final scene.

quotations.text: Whoe'er I woo, myself would be his wife.
quotations.speaker: Viola
quotations.context: An aside, having agreed to carry Orsino's suit to Olivia.
quotations.analysis: One rhymed line closes the scene and states the play's central knot for the first time. Three days into her employment she is already in the position the rest of the comedy depends on, and she tells the audience, nobody on stage — which is where she will keep it for four acts.

quotations.text: Oh, you are sick of self-love, Malvolio, and taste with a distempered appetite.
quotations.speaker: Olivia
quotations.context: Rebuking her steward for sneering at Feste's wit.
quotations.analysis: The diagnosis is delivered in the same appetite imagery Orsino used in the first scene, so the play's two kinds of self-absorption are made to rhyme. It is also the reason the forged letter will work: his mistress has told him publicly what his weakness is, and Maria is listening.

quotations.text: Make me a willow cabin at your gate, And call upon my soul within the house; Write loyal cantons of contemned love And sing them loud even in the dead of night;
quotations.speaker: Viola
quotations.context: Answering Olivia's question: what would you do if you loved as your master does?
quotations.analysis: Asked what she would do, she describes a courtship nobody in the play is actually conducting — noisy, sleepless, unembarrassed — and it is the moment Olivia falls. The irony is exact: the speech is convincing because Viola means it, and she means it about somebody else.

quotations.text: Disguise, I see, thou art a wickedness, Wherein the pregnant enemy does much.
quotations.speaker: Viola
quotations.context: Alone, having realised what Olivia's returned ring means.
quotations.analysis: She blames the costume, not herself, and the ‘pregnant enemy’ is the devil, ready and resourceful. It is the only moral judgement anybody passes on the disguise in the whole play, and she passes it on herself before anyone else has noticed there is a problem.

quotations.text: How will this fadge? my master loves her dearly; And I, poor monster, fond as much on him; And she, mistaken, seems to dote on me.
quotations.speaker: Viola
quotations.context: The same soliloquy, setting out the triangle.
quotations.analysis: ‘Monster’ is the word she chooses for being both man and woman, and it is harsher than anything her enemies say about her. The three clauses are perfectly parallel, which makes the impasse look like a diagram: everyone is loving in the right direction and at the wrong person.

quotations.text: O time! thou must untangle this, not I; It is too hard a knot for me to untie!
quotations.speaker: Viola
quotations.context: The couplet that ends the soliloquy and the scene.
quotations.analysis: The cleverest person in the play admits she has no plan, and the comedy takes her at her word: nothing she does resolves anything, and the knot is cut by her brother walking on stage in Act V. It is an unusual thing for a Shakespearean protagonist to say, and the play never contradicts it.

quotations.text: Trip no further, pretty sweeting; Journeys end in lovers meeting, Every wise man's son doth know.
quotations.speaker: Feste
quotations.context: Singing 'O mistress mine' to Sir Toby and Sir Andrew at midnight.
quotations.analysis: A love song sung to two drunks by a professional, ending on the flattest possible authority — every wise man's son knows it, which is to say it is a commonplace. The next stanza's point is that youth does not last, and the play's three marriages are all arranged by people in a hurry.

quotations.text: Art any more than a steward? Dost thou think, because thou art virtuous, there shall be no more cakes and ale?
quotations.speaker: Sir Toby
quotations.context: To Malvolio, who has come down in his nightgown to stop the singing.
quotations.analysis: Two questions, and the first one is the real argument: rank, not morality, is what Sir Toby thinks settles the matter. The line is often quoted as a defence of pleasure against puritanism, but in context it is a gentleman telling a servant to remember his place, and the joke depends on that as much as on the ale.

quotations.text: A blank, my lord. She never told her love, But let concealment, like a worm i' the bud, Feed on her damask cheek: she pined in thought, And with a green and yellow melancholy She sat like patience on a monument, Smiling at grief.
quotations.speaker: Viola
quotations.context: Asked by Orsino for the history of the sister she has just invented.
quotations.analysis: She describes her own situation to the man responsible for it, in the third person and the past tense, and he asks whether the girl died. 'A blank' is the exact word for a history nobody was told, and the statue image is chosen for stillness: she is describing the one thing she is not allowed to do, which is act.

quotations.text: I am all the daughters of my father's house, And all the brothers too: and yet I know not.
quotations.speaker: Viola
quotations.context: Answering Orsino's question of whether her sister died of love.
quotations.analysis: The sentence is literally true, riddling and heartbreaking: she is the only surviving child and, in her clothes, both the daughter and the son. ‘And yet I know not’ is her hedge about her brother’s death, and it is the nearest she comes to hope in the first half of the play.

quotations.text: be not afraid of greatness: some are born great, some achieve greatness, and some have greatness thrust upon 'em.
quotations.speaker: Malvolio
quotations.context: Reading Maria's forged letter aloud in the garden, watched from behind a box-tree.
quotations.analysis: Maria's cleverest stroke is that the sentence says nothing at all: it covers every possible route upward and so confirms whichever one the reader already believes in. Feste quotes it back at him in the last scene, and a flattering commonplace becomes the epitaph of the joke.

quotations.text: Then think you right: I am not what I am.
quotations.speaker: Viola
quotations.context: To Olivia, who has just said she thinks the same of Cesario.
quotations.analysis: It is a confession that cannot be heard as one, and it is deliberately a step short of a lie. The formula inverts the name God gives himself in Exodus, and Shakespeare gives the same construction to Iago; here it costs its speaker something instead of arming her.

quotations.text: Love sought is good, but given unsought better.
quotations.speaker: Olivia
quotations.context: Declaring herself to Cesario, having abandoned discretion.
quotations.analysis: She makes a proverb out of her own position — unasked love is worth more — at the moment she is doing the asking. The line is a rhymed couplet in a scene that slips back and forth between prose and verse, and the shift into sententious rhyme is exactly how a formal woman gives herself permission.

quotations.text: Nothing that is so is so.
quotations.speaker: Feste
quotations.context: To Sebastian, whom he takes for Cesario and who denies knowing him.
quotations.analysis: Six words that state the plot: the fool is mistaken about the man in front of him and is nevertheless exactly right about the world he is in. He arrives at the formula by a run of sarcastic denials, which means the truest sentence in the play is produced by accident.

quotations.text: Or I am mad, or else this is a dream:
quotations.speaker: Sebastian
quotations.context: After Olivia has stopped the brawl and invited him into her house.
quotations.analysis: He is offered a countess, a household and a marriage by a stranger, and his response is to check his own sanity — the same question the household is at that moment putting to Malvolio in the dark. The play runs both tests in the same act and reaches opposite verdicts.

quotations.text: Madman, thou errest: I say, there is no darkness but ignorance; in which thou art more puzzled than the Egyptians in their fog.
quotations.speaker: Feste
quotations.context: Disguised as Sir Topas the curate, speaking to Malvolio through the door of a dark room.
quotations.analysis: The proposition is a scholastic commonplace and it is being used to gaslight a man who has correctly observed that he is shut in the dark. Feste has put on a false beard nobody can see, which makes this the one disguise in the play worn purely for the pleasure of the wearer.

quotations.text: An apple, cleft in two, is not more twin Than these two creatures. Which is Sebastian?
quotations.speaker: Antonio
quotations.context: Seeing Viola and Sebastian on stage together for the first time.
quotations.analysis: The recognition is given not to the twins or the lovers but to Antonio, who has most to lose by it — he has just been calling Viola a traitor. The homely image of a cut apple lands in the middle of the play's most formal verse, and his question is the one the whole comedy has been withholding.

quotations.text: and thus the whirligig of time brings in his revenges.
quotations.speaker: Feste
quotations.context: Revealing to Malvolio that he was Sir Topas, and reminding him of his own insults.
quotations.analysis: A whirligig is a child's spinning toy, which makes cosmic justice into something that goes round because somebody set it going. He has been waiting since Act I for this, and the sentence admits that the punishment was personal, not corrective.

quotations.text: I'll be revenged on the whole pack of you.
quotations.speaker: Malvolio
quotations.context: His exit line, leaving the final scene.
quotations.analysis: The last words of the only character who refuses the comedy's settlement, and he walks off stage with them unanswered. Olivia's reply — that he has been most notoriously abused — concedes the point, and Orsino sends somebody after him, which is not the same as putting it right.

quotations.text: When that I was and a little tiny boy, With hey, ho, the wind and the rain, A foolish thing was but a toy, For the rain it raineth every day.
quotations.speaker: Feste
quotations.context: Alone on the empty stage after everyone else has gone in.
quotations.analysis: The song walks a life from childhood to marriage to drunkenness to old age, and each stanza ends with the same weather. It is the only Shakespearean comedy that finishes with a solitary figure singing about how little difference the ending has made, and the refrain is what the audience takes out into the street.

timeline.label: Barnabe Riche's Farewell to Military Profession
timeline.detail: Contains 'Of Apolonius and Silla', the twin-and-disguise tale that is the play's chief source.

timeline.label: The play is most likely written
timeline.detail: Dated by its style and by the fact that it was already being performed early in 1602.

timeline.label: Performed at Middle Temple Hall
timeline.detail: On 2 February, recorded in the diary of the law student John Manningham — the earliest surviving notice of the play.

timeline.label: First Folio
timeline.detail: Printed among the comedies as Twelfe Night, Or what you will; there is no earlier text.

timeline.label: Harley Granville-Barker's Savoy production
timeline.detail: A fast, uncut staging on a simple set that helped end the tradition of heavy Victorian scenery in Shakespeare.

timeline.label: John Barton's production for the Royal Shakespeare Company
timeline.detail: An autumnal, melancholy reading that shaped how the play was staged for a generation.

timeline.label: Trevor Nunn's film
timeline.detail: A screen version that opens with the shipwreck and gives the Malvolio plot its full weight.

timeline.label: An all-male staging at Shakespeare's Globe
timeline.detail: Original-practices costume and casting, with Mark Rylance as Olivia, revived a decade later in the West End and on Broadway.

places.name: The Illyrian coast
places.note: Illyria was the old name for the eastern Adriatic shore; Shakespeare uses it as a place far enough away to be anything he needs.

places.name: Middle Temple Hall, London
places.note: Where the play's earliest recorded performance was given on 2 February 1602.

places.name: Southwark, London
places.note: Antonio's inn, the Elephant in the south suburbs, borrows the name of a real establishment on the theatre side of the river.

places.name: Ware, Hertfordshire
places.note: Sir Toby tells Sir Andrew to write a challenge as big as the Great Bed of Ware, a celebrated inn bed and a standing English joke.

criticalViews.summary: Read through its title, the play belongs to the end of the Christmas holiday: misrule is licensed, a steward is mocked, appetites are indulged, and ordinary order returns at the close with three marriages.
criticalViews.counter: The holiday reading has to account for a final scene in which one character leaves swearing revenge and another is left alone singing about rain.

criticalViews.position: A play about gender and desire
criticalViews.summary: Much recent criticism concentrates on the fact that Orsino falls in love with Cesario and proposes while still calling her by that name, and on Olivia's attraction to a woman. The disguise is the condition of the real feeling, not a delay before it.
criticalViews.counter: The play still ends in the conventional pairings, and Viola’s own language about her disguise is uneasy, not liberating.

criticalViews.summary: Since the eighteenth century the steward has drawn as much attention as the lovers, and productions differ over whether the dark-room scenes are broad comedy or an early study of cruelty licensed by a group.
criticalViews.counter: Malvolio is also genuinely unpleasant to almost everyone before the trick begins, and the play gives Maria and Feste real provocation.

essayQuestions.question: How does Shakespeare use disguise in Twelfth Night?
plan: Begin with the practical origin of the disguise in 1.2 — it is protection and employment before it is anything else.
Show how it lets truth out: the willow-cabin speech and the sister who never told her love.
Use 2.2 and 3.1 to trace Viola's own judgement on the costume, from wickedness to 'I am not what I am'.
Compare Feste's beard in 4.2, a disguise nobody can see, and ask what it is for.
Close on the last scene: she never changes back on stage, and Orsino goes on calling her Cesario.

essayQuestions.question: Is the treatment of Malvolio funny?
essayQuestions.focus: Festivity, cruelty and the limits of a joke
plan: Establish the provocation: he is rude to Feste in 1.5 and to the whole household in 2.3, and he is right about the noise.
Analyse why the letter works — it tells him what Olivia has already told him he believes about himself.
Mark the change of register at 4.2, where a prank becomes confinement and a fake priest denies the evidence of his senses.
Weigh the last scene: Olivia calls it notorious abuse, Fabian explains it away, and Feste admits the revenge was personal.
Decide what a production owes him, and what is lost if he is played as sympathetic throughout.

essayQuestions.question: Discuss the presentation of love in the play.
essayQuestions.focus: Imagination, constancy and the speed of feeling
plan: Open with Orsino's appetite imagery in 1.1 and the fact that he has never met Olivia.
Set against it Olivia's instant reversal in 1.5 and Sebastian's acceptance of a marriage in 4.3.
Use 2.4 to show Viola’s love as the one the play defines by waiting, not speaking.
Add Antonio, whose attachment to Sebastian is the most costly in the play and gets no ending at all.
Judge whether the three marriages are a resolution or simply where the music stops.

essayQuestions.question: What does Feste contribute to Twelfth Night?
essayQuestions.focus: The fool, the songs and the play's ending
plan: Note first that he is employed, paid by two houses, and absent without leave when the play begins.
Show his professional method in 1.5 and 3.1 — proof by wordplay, and the claim that words have been corrupted.
Read the songs as a sequence: 'O mistress mine', 'Come away, death', and the final ballad.
Examine his part in 4.2 and his return to it at 5.1.384, where he names his own motive.
Conclude with the empty stage: what does it mean that a comedy ends with its fool alone?

discussionQuestions: Orsino proposes to a person he has known only as Cesario. Has he fallen in love with Viola, or with the servant?
Olivia mourns for seven years and abandons it in one scene. Is the play laughing at her, or at mourning?
Where exactly does the joke on Malvolio stop being funny, and can a production put the line somewhere else?
Antonio is given no partner and no explanation in the final scene. What should he be doing while the marriages are arranged?
The play ends with a song about rain, not a dance. What does that do to everything before it?

related.why: The comedy just before it, and the other one where a gulling scene played for laughs runs beyond what its victims can forgive.
The other great disguise comedy of these years, where the heroine’s boy’s clothes buy her freedom and do not trap her.
Shakespeare's early twin play, and the plainest demonstration of how much the device changes when the twins are brother and sister.
Another play that begins with a shipwreck and ends with a reunion, written at the far end of Shakespeare's career.
A comedy that also leaves one character outside its happy ending, and leaves the audience to decide what to do about him.
